name: rocq
why: The Coq proof assistant renamed; running formal proofs and dependent types is a real mathematical rabbit hole.

brief.what_it_is: Rocq (formerly the Coq Proof Assistant) is an interactive theorem prover and dependently-typed programming language. You write definitions, executable algorithms, theorems and proof scripts in its formal language, and it checks the proofs with a small trusted kernel. It can also extract executable programs from specifications as OCaml or Haskell source. The Homebrew description calls it a proof assistant for higher-order logic, but the homepage and README describe a dependent type theory, so the brew blurb undersells it. The installed executables include coqc, coqtop, rocq, coqchk, coqdep, coqdoc and votour.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a tool 'to write mathematical definitions, executable algorithms and theorems together with an environment for semi-interactive development of machine-checked proofs'. The homepage pitches it as a trustworthy, industrial-strength tool for mechanised reasoning in mathematics, computer science and more.
brief.how_it_works: Proofs are built interactively with tactics and checked by a kernel written in OCaml, which the homepage describes as a well-delimited, trusted core. The homepage says the core type theory is formalised in the MetaRocq project and that a verified reference checker can be extracted to shrink the trusted base. Compiled output comes from the coqc/rocq compilers, and the native conversion checker relies on the OCaml runtime.

commands_seen.context: Prints the Rocq version. The README suggests including it in bug reports.
Same as coqtop -v, using the new rocq entry point, to report the version in bug reports.

brief.install_notes: Linux: the official Rocq Platform binary installer is no longer offered, so the Platform is installed from source via its scripts, which wrap opam. Also available: the experimental Rocq Platform Starter GUI installer (it also sets up VS Code and VsRocq), opam directly, Nix, distro packages (the version may be old and external packages may be missing), and Docker. macOS: the Platform binary installer (recommended for beginners), the scripts, Homebrew (limited external packages), Nix, or Docker. Windows: the Platform binary installer, the scripts (run them first so opam environment variables are set), or WSL or a Linux VM. Editors: VsRocq is the recommended VS Code extension and needs a matching language server version; alternatives are Rocq LSP, VsCoq Legacy, Proof General plus Company-Coq for Emacs, Coqtail for Vim/Neovim, and the standalone RocqIDE. Bug reports should cite the OCaml version, Rocq version and configuration.
brief.standout: The homepage ships live code samples (fac, a lemma proved with lia, extraction to OCaml) and it is the lineage of Coq, with decades of use in the Four Colour Theorem, CompCert and HoTT. Its MetaRocq project verifies the kernel's own type theory.
brief.status: Maintained. The homepage lists Rocq Prover 9.2.0 (2026-03-27) and Rocq Platform 2026.07.0 (2026-07-30). The GitHub README shows active GitLab and GitHub CI badges, a Zenodo DOI, and a live reference manual for master. I did not see a commit date.
brief.caveats: native_compute is only supported on some x86 setups when built with OCaml 5, according to the 9.2.0 release notes. There is no Linux binary installer for the Platform. The Homebrew route lacks many external packages and has no language server, so VS Code users need VsCoq Legacy. The VsRocq extension and language server must be the same version. The brew description ('higher-order logic') is looser than the project's own framing. I did not check the license, and the homepage text I read did not state it.
quotes: A trustworthy, industrial-strength interactive theorem prover and dependently-typed programming language for mechanised reasoning in mathematics, computer science and more.
The Rocq Prover was formerly known as the Coq Proof Assistant (see more on the name evolution).
It provides a formal language to write mathematical definitions, executable algorithms and theorems together with an environment for semi-interactive development of machine-checked proofs.
